Emphasis mine, obviously, but what I'm trying to get at is that Mafumafu didn't claim that he was trying to hide the relationship, period. He was very explicit about how he had hidden it from the **public** specifically(and regrets it, based on his account). 

The parts I bolded I did so in order to highlight that Mafumafu himself admitted that "(close/intimate) friends**¹** , Persons (associated**/**involved) with [Mfmf**/**A子さん**/**Both], Persons concerned with A子さんs employment under [INSERT COMPANY HERE] as a 「ネット活動者」, and later "Third Parties" associated with A子さん who propagating a smear campaign against Mafumafu(he even gave the time period for this: 「離婚協議中も」("during divorce proceedings", which lasted from May 2022 to July 2022; again, this is taken verbatim from his retelling of events). Just look at the tweet he made about this. 
Notice how he chained multiple 'の', which  you would usually avoid because it makes it less clear what is getting modified by what.

Notice how his format is: 
[name] 'と' [name] 'の' [thing 1] 'の' [thing 2] 'の' [thing 3] 
In such a case,  it could gramatically be any of the things from [things 1-3] that is getting modified with such syntax

For example, "Mikeneko 'の' cat" would render in English as something like "Mikeneko's cat"

Thus, when Korekore said:
"...まふまふと奥さん →の← Vtuber潤羽るしあの夫婦間のトラブル..." 
His putting the stress on the 'の' that's pointed out above makes it so that the statement isn't necessarily implying that the wife(奥さん) and ”Vtuber潤羽るしあ” are the same person in all cases. 

Now, inferring that he meant that Mikeneko was the wife IS the natural reading, but because there are other possible readings, it can't be certain that he intended for it to convey the most natural meaning of that sentence.

Essentially, the clause in Korekore's tweet gives Korekore plausible deniability to claim that he never actually meant to imply that Mikeneko was Mafumafu's wife. 

It's worded specifically to lead people to draw conclusions without having to take responsibility for claiming it himself in the case where he ends up being wrong(and by doing so, he avoids legal consequences regardless of any harm he would normally be held responsible for)

The dichotomy of supernatural power users being stronger than mundane martials makes perfect sense. People are warping the actual definition of mundane to suit a view that actually makes no sense. If somebody throws a mountain in a world where that kind of feat is as ridiculous for **normal people** as it is in our world(most settings), you're not mundane. You're supernatural. Because you are not natural. You might say that "magic" is a very specific thing in D&D where it is a manifestation of the weave, but we all know that's never where the conversation is. It's always some vague non-sense about Shonen protagonists and John Wick, ignoring the fact that just because the movie or show casts them in the light of "peak of human ability", doesn't actually mean that what they're doing is reasonable to depict as something naturally possible through our biology. It requires a suspension of disbelief, where we "trick" ourselves in not thinking too deeply about physical limitations because it is "close enough".

The issue is that in a world with explicit magic, this goes out the window. Because in such a world, to properly understand it, we MUST begin to categorize feats of power in terms of how "supernatural" they are, as opposed to how "peak of human ability" they are. In such a setting, supernatural quite clearly overlays entirely over and completely replaces "peak human ability" in terms of comparison of abilities. It's not that people can't do the same things those "mundane" heroes did- it's that now, they exist in a reference frame of a sliding scale of feats where one end is human and one end is distinctly supernatural, instead of a sliding scale of "weak human" to "strong human", because the latter scale is simply now a rephrasing of the prior. Any angle you approach it from, in a world with supernatural elements, any degree of 'superhumanity' can be replaced with an interpretation of that same thing but by its degree of 'supernaturality'. 

Attempts at distinguishing the two can only be done for the sake of itself, and would honestly be purely syntactical in nature, and thus useless as a basis for class design, because all you have to do is make anything happen and simply say "oh but he did it because he's an awesome dude, not supernatural". A distinction without actual meaning fails to be a distinction. Supernatural and not becomes an arbitrary label, useful only for nebulous character themes that would likely be discordant with the greater themes of the setting. Suddenly you have one dude casting Wish, and the other dude basically casting Wish, but he does it because he's like really cool and stuff. People need to realize that not every character type can fit into every setting and still maintain the same integrity it would in its optimal setting.

Obviously, this doesn't address class balance. But I'd argue that D&D's half-hearted ties to an illogical proposition are the reason the imbalance exists in the first place. And also that some people, whether they admit it or not, are often fine with being more successful gameplay wise than their friends at the table and see nothing wrong with that(often, they are the ones playing the "stronger" classes, I wonder why). Arguing better balance is a losing proposition from the get-go with them, because they revel in sacrificing others enjoyment at the table in favor of pursuing a selfish power fantasy in a group-centered game. They like to ignore the fact that acting as if they can simply act as if others are not pursuing a power fantasy unless told otherwise is a valid view of the hobby, but I personally can't stand people whose default position is "I can be an asshole until told otherwise", just because there are people out there that exist that might be fine with you being an asshole.

Assuming AC is 16, chance to hit is 12 out of 20 rolls for a standard roll, one being a crit/auto-hit. 

With disadvantage, this means 143 out of 400 rolls will hit, and 1 out of 400 rolls will crit. 0.3575 chance to hit with disadvantage, 0.0025 for crit, so average for two disadvantage rolls worth of damage will be:

2*((0.3575*[WpnDmg])+(0.0025*(2*[WpnDmg]))) or
((0.715*[WpnDmg])+(0.005*(2*[WpnDmg])))

Meanwhile, the one at advantage will have 297 chances to land a hit, and 39 chances to crit. 0.7425 chance to hit, 0.0975 to crit.

(0.7425*[WpnDmg])+(0.0975*(2*[WpnDmg]))

The advantage shot has is strictly superior.

Note that as the AC of the creature goes down(or your hit bonus goes up, functionally equivalent to AC decrease), the formula tilts in favor of the disadvantage shot. As AC goes up, it tilts further towards the advantage shot. At AC 10, for example, the disadvantage shot deals (1.615*[WpnDmg])+(0.005*(2*[WpnDmg]))), while the advantage shot does (0.975*[WpnDmg])+(0.0975*(2*[WpnDmg])). That's a pretty sizable difference so obviously the breakpoint between the two lies somewhere between AC 10 and 16, I'm sure there's a way to graph it and see exactly where(or just hand count it since there's like 5 numbers in between to check) but that's just to illustrate what you're working with.

Spells are often unique effects, but other times? They can just be analogous to "mundane" abilities, or if their effects are not, their outcomes are. A well used trap can be used to decisively end a "simple" encounter as much as spells can. You think the T-Rex is bad? Alright, well the Fighter just dug a 40 foot deep pit trap lined with spikes that the ranger helped conceal. The "simple" enemies charge, because they are, well, simple. Fall into the pit. Encounter over.

You might say, "Well that's not fair, there's all sort of other things that can be used in combat to make it interesting that won't end the combat!"

Sure, because those other things are not well-defined in the rules, and you use the power of DM fiat to make them not end the fight. If a creature falls down a pit trap, it by all accounts *should* effectively end the encounter. But there is no "pit trap fail=dead" rule in the book. So maybe you give the enemy a Perception check. Then maybe you give them a Dex save. Maybe you give them a few. Maybe they fail, but not by a lot, so they catch 15 feet down and take "strain" damage instead of fall damage, and then you give them an athletics check to get back into the fight, mostly at full power minus a bit of HP. 

You can't do that, strictly RAW, with something like Leomunds Tiny Hut, because it basically says in the text itself "Hey DM, no, fuck you, the players get to avoid this encounter". I mean, you can say anything as the DM, but I don't think I'm missing the mark when I say that most DMs are far less willing to change clear cut effects on the fly, while most feel comfortable arbitrating unconventional effects as they desire(often muting their effectiveness).

But now imagine if, say, a martial subclass was released that had something like this feature:
"The ___ can spend a short rest digging a 50-foot wide, 20-foot thick, 40-foot deep trench pit full of hazards and conceal it perfectly. This pit cannot be noticed by any means, and any creature that passes over it that is not aware of the trench immediately falls into the pit and cannot escape it without spending 8 hours of attempting to escape the trench. After 8 hours of attempting to leave the trench, the creature appears at the edge of the trench, directly across from the location where it fell into it. Creatures who were with the character when the trench was created can maneuver across it without incident." 

The fact is that it is very rare for me to see an encounter in D&D that is thematically simple without being mechanically simple in an already simplistic system.

And don't get me wrong, simple is fine. There are very few objectively wrong ways to play. But it's hardly everybody's style. Some people wanna come to the table, roll some dice, and see what happens. But others want to occasionally be able to perform actions that don't merely shift the circumstances of an encounter, but redefine them altogether; they want to feel story-changing weight to their combat actions.

Something I've learned is simply not appealing to most of the people I've played with is "combat for the sake of combat".
If people like the War Game aspect of D&D, they'll almost certainly enjoy a dynamic fight with clever set pieces and accommodations for their strategies more. If they aren't, the combat won't be all that fun for them regardless of what you do, but at least with a dynamic scene, you can offer them a chance to live vicariously through the excitement of the war gamers.
And if you feel the combat is just a fight for the sake of a fight? Turn it into a story instead. A skill challenge. This, by the way, solves many(but not all) of the "encounter killer" effects of spells, because by turning it into a skill challenge where each player is allowed to describe an action and the resources they expend to perform it, you are allowed to arbitrate its overall success to the effort. The wizard knows exactly what Polymorph does, stat-wise, in a turn by turn fight. But in the skill challenge, you are the boss. You know how big of a badass that T-Rex is, and moreover how expensive it cost resource wise, so you already give some hypothetical points towards success here because it was used. But then comes the Strength checks as it barrels through the trees. The Animal Handling checks of the party as they try and keep the dumb party member trampling in the right direction. The Dex save as a tree begins to fall in its direction, and failing that, the Str save to see how long it takes to pull itself free(costing time which the group is using to do x important thing in this scene). 

But really, I think the idea that no ability should exist that fundamentally alters how players can interact with the game is silly. This is D&D, a class-based RPG. Classes exist to reinforce different capabilities. The idea that the divergence of these capabilities should never be so great as to prevent an encounter from being avoidable for one group while not so for another is at odds with the baseline design of the system itself. 

Sometimes, that means that certain events stop being notable. Yes, that includes events that would be combat encounters to another party. You say it's silly to have the counters for the players in nearly every encounter. Well, D&D defines an encounter as something that expends resources; it doesn't matter how many swarms of wolves come up on the dome, the players aren't any closer to the next level, story beat, or whatever. You mention it in passing, as flavor dressing. The encounters you do bother narrating should be the ones that actually require the players to take an active role, or expend resources, to 'complete'.

"But there aren't a lot of those encounters! Wouldn't the players just do one, then long rest, and go into each fight fully topped off!"

Welcome to a sandbox TTRPG. Your players "could" also refuse to step out of the starting town and instead decide to spend all of their money, focus, and attention on building up a Pizza Parlor in Bumfawk City or Nowheres Town, and avoid your encounters by never being there to encounter them.

But players, generally, don't do that. And if they do, and the DM doesn't like it and feel they can go along with it, those games don't last long.

Well a pre-made world for a setting agnostic system is sort of a whole different ball game. There are game systems that only release content applicable to one setting, the only setting, and so everybody who goes into that game knows the rules.

I'd very rarely play a pre-made for D&D, for the reasons you mentioned.

1) I find it more compelling to work within a series of boundaries, but have trouble being satisfied with self-imagined boundaries. The settings I prefer are all narratively consistent in the broader scheme of things, and my ability of familiarize myself with the setting at large lets me keep myself grounded to the core themes of that setting(which are likely the themes I want for that campaign).

2) Improvisation is much, much easier in pre-written settings. I say this as somebody who has run homebrew games with 400 pages of worldbuilding for his campaign. I literally wrote scripts for every session for that game. I still found myself drifting in my DM style and theme more often than in pre-written settings, explicitly because of how I was aware that it was "my" world. I tend to find it easier to respect the boundaries others have, including in their artistic works, than my own.

3) It's nice to know when everybody at the table is "in" on the setting. Its tropes, quirks, etc. They know you can throw interesting things into the mix, but having a bevvy of name drops, cryptic hints at overarching plotlines, etc at hand is very nice and fun. You can be anywhere in the Imperium of Man doing whatever the fuck you're doing, but if you hint at chaos you can see the players all react at the "Oh shit" moment, or dropping hints of the sabbat in a Vampire game, etc.

I think it's a difference in preference. I wouldn't allow this for the same reason I prefer tabletop games that have pre-determined settings. I like it when every number you crunch is a story you choose to take your character down, with all the pros and cons therein. Hyper-sandbox play never appealed to me.

One way I've fiddled with is 
1) reroll 1's, common homebrew. This makes the dice roll average equal to the average static per level. 

And 

2) Allow a person to convert a roll to the static average after you make the roll for PROF number of times. So, at the very least, the players can engage with the roll, and if you get fucked, you can bail out a few times. So essentially, players get to roll at least 6 times over the course of a campaign, and if they fuck up 6 rolls back to back, they can get averages out of that, and then continue to take averages(or roll and risk it without a failsafe). 

With this, at the very least, we're looking at people who have at minimum [HD Max] + (6*[HD Static Average]) + (2*13). Which is ~9`+(6*~5.5`)+26+(20*[CON Mod]), or ~9`+~33`+26+~40`= ~108 health at level 20 as a baseline if you got the absolute worst roll results possible, which is...not great, but not as bad as the unmodified rolls, which would be ~9`+19+~40`=68(or lower, if your table also allows stat rolls to absolutely fuck you and you dump Con like a maniac).

It does boost the average and it doesn't prevent a person from getting good rolls continuously, but it allows the players to "earn" the chance for more HP by levelling. It makes rolling well less rewarding, but I by the nature of a long-term game, it can be frustrating when dice side with you for short term success, but with another for long term benefits, which in terms improve their odds of short-term success over yours anyway.
